sections.heading: Holding me steady when ministry feels heavy
sections.text: Unchanging Lord, when I am discouraged in ministry and full of doubts about myself, plant my feet again on the rock of your eternal choice in Christ. Keep my hands from dropping in defeat. Give me hope for my own soul, and hope that you can bring others to life through service as weak as mine.
theological_themes: God is unchanging and faithful when the minister feels unstable.
God’s gracious election gives courage because salvation rests on him, not on human strength.
Ministry hope comes from God’s power, not the minister’s confidence.

scripture_references.connection: Paul grounds the believer’s salvation in God’s gracious choosing in Christ before the foundation of the world. That makes election a source of worship, humility, and steadiness rather than a reason for pride.
Paul endures ministry hardship because he trusts that God will bring salvation to his elect people through the gospel. This connects God’s sovereign purpose with real perseverance in service.

sections.heading: Trusting you to call your people
sections.text: Father, you know your people one by one. At the time you have appointed, you call them out of what they are by nature and bring them into the life of grace. Let this be the ground of my salvation, the desire of my heart, and the reason I keep serving.
theological_themes: God personally knows those who belong to him.
God effectually calls sinners from spiritual death into grace.
The minister’s work is motivated by confidence in God’s saving action.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes himself as the shepherd who knows his sheep and brings them in. This supports the prayer’s confidence that God personally knows and gathers his people.

Paul links God’s foreknowing, predestining, calling, justifying, and glorifying as one sure work of salvation. The passage grounds the prayer’s trust that God’s appointed call truly brings his people to grace.

This passage describes sinners as spiritually dead by nature and made alive by God’s mercy. It gives biblical shape to the prayer’s language of being brought from a natural condition into a gracious one.

sections.heading: Keeping me low and honest before you
sections.text: Keep me from thinking too highly of myself or my work. Apart from you, I bring sin and weakness; even the best things I do are mixed with motives that need mercy. Humble me deeply before you. Pull out self-righteousness like a poisonous weed. Show me how empty I am without your grace. Keep me aware that I am a sinner who lives only by your mercy, and lead me into real repentance.
theological_themes: Human weakness and indwelling sin make self-confidence dangerous.
Self-righteousness must be exposed and rooted out.
True ministry requires humility, repentance, and dependence on grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul speaks honestly about the inability of the flesh to produce true good before God. This supports the prayer’s confession that, apart from God’s grace, the minister has no ground for confidence in himself.
Paul rejects any righteousness of his own and wants to be found in Christ. This directly illuminates the prayer’s request to have self-righteousness torn out and replaced with dependence on grace.
Jesus contrasts self-exalting religion with the humble cry of a sinner for mercy. The prayer follows the tax collector’s posture rather than the Pharisee’s confidence in himself.

sections.heading: Tearing down the pride I keep rebuilding
sections.text: Break the idol of pride in me the way Dagon fell before your ark. Pull down the little tower of Babel I build out of my own opinions. Flatten the Jericho walls of my stubborn, rebellious heart. When all of that is down, let my experience and my cry be this: grace, grace, and nothing but grace.
theological_themes: Pride is idolatrous and cannot stand before God’s presence.
Self-exalting plans and opinions must be brought down by God.
Grace becomes precious when pride is demolished.

scripture_references.connection: Dagon falling before the ark is a vivid picture of false gods collapsing before the presence of the true God. The prayer uses that image to ask God to overthrow inward pride as an idol.
Babel shows humanity trying to build a name for itself apart from submission to God. This supports the prayer’s plea for God to scatter self-exalting ambition and self-opinion.
James teaches that God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble, calling believers to humble themselves before him. That pattern matches the prayer’s movement from broken pride to grace.

sections.heading: Leaning on your strength when my faith is weak
sections.text: When my faith is not active, I am weak and earthbound, like an eagle with tied wings. Help me rest on your power and your faithfulness, not on my energy, gifts, plans, or reputation. Teach me again what is worth living for: to see your cause move forward in the world, and to do real good to people’s souls and bodies.
theological_themes: Faith must actively rely on God’s power and faithfulness.
Weakness in ministry is met by divine strength.
Christian service includes both spiritual care and practical good for others.

scripture_references.connection: Paul learns that Christ’s power is displayed in weakness, so weakness becomes a place of dependence rather than despair. This grounds the prayer’s request to serve from God’s strength instead of personal ability.
Paul urges believers not to grow weary in doing good and to do good to all as they have opportunity. This supports the prayer’s desire to serve people in concrete ways, not only in words.
Peter frames ministry gifts as stewardship from God and calls servants to serve by the strength God supplies. This connects usefulness in ministry with dependence on God’s power.

sections.heading: Keeping me faithful to the end
sections.text: Father, make this my ministry, my life, my prayer, and my aim. Give me the grace I need so I do not fail, give up, or make peace with unfaithfulness. Hold me, strengthen me, and make me useful until the work you have given me is done.
theological_themes: The minister’s life is to be spent for God’s mission and the good of others.
Perseverance in ministry depends on God’s sustaining grace.
Faithfulness to the end is a gift God must give.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes his life as valuable only insofar as he finishes the ministry entrusted to him by the Lord Jesus. This closely matches the prayer’s desire for ministry, life, prayer, and final aim to be one.
Paul labors for the spiritual maturity of others, but he does so with God’s energy working in him. The passage holds together strenuous ministry and dependence on grace.
Jude ends by praising God as the one able to keep his people from stumbling. This supports the final plea that God would give grace so the minister does not fail.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The prayer’s appeal to eternal election and effectual calling reflects a distinctly Reformed soteriology; these doctrines are historically orthodox but contested among Christians.

The original’s language that the minister is “nothing but sin and weakness” and that his “best works are but sin” is intentionally severe Puritan language. I rendered it as sin and mixed motives apart from grace so as to preserve the confession of corruption without implying that the Holy Spirit produces nothing genuinely good in believers.

The phrase “self-abhorrence” can be pastorally misunderstood as unhealthy self-hatred. I retained the force by speaking of deep humility, repentance, and the collapse of self-righteousness before God.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated “fasten me upon the rock of thy eternal election” as a request for stability in God’s saving purpose, not as a call to speculate about who is elect.
I rendered “natural to a gracious state” as being called out of what we are by nature into the life of grace, drawing on Ephesians 2 to keep the original’s theological meaning accessible.

I kept the concrete biblical images of Dagon, Babel, and Jericho rather than replacing them with abstractions, but expressed them as images of pride, self-opinion, and a rebellious heart being brought down before God.
I translated “souls and bodies of men” as “people’s souls and bodies” to preserve the original concern for whole-person ministry without retaining gendered generic language.
